message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
## Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

**Bottom line.** The bid rests on a real local pilot, and the Sunday results are strong. But the costing table doesn't add up to the amount requested. The headline evening claim is contradicted by Table 1. The visit and cost-per-visit figures assume all five branches perform like the busiest one. The self-service comparison doesn't show what the author says it shows. All of this can be fixed, but Members shouldn't be asked to approve the bid as written.

### 1. The total is £10,000 too high

Table 2 lists £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = **£164,000**, not £174,000. Either a line is missing or the total is wrong. In a growth bid, this is the first thing a finance officer or Member will check.

The individual lines are calculated correctly: 10 × 2 × 50 × 5 = 5,000 hours, at £24.80 = £124,000.

### 2. Evening demand is well below daytime, not "close to" it

From Table 1:

| Slot | Visits per hour | Share of weekday daytime average (53.5) |
|---|---|---|
| Tuesday/Thursday evening (new) | 21 | 39% |
| Sunday (new) | 52 | 97% |

The weekday daytime average is (3 × 46 + 5 × 58) ÷ 8 = 53.5 visits per hour. Evening use runs at about two-fifths of that. Sunday is the slot that comes close to daytime levels. The document repeats the evening claim in Sections 3 and 8, and the author's description repeats it again. It needs correcting in all three places.

This changes the case. Using staffing cost alone, per branch:
- **Sunday:** £9,920 for about 10,400 visits, roughly **£0.95 per visit**.
- **Evenings:** £14,880 for about 6,300 visits, roughly **£2.36 per visit**.

Sunday opening is clearly well supported. Evening opening is weaker, though the job club shows it has value beyond visit counts.

### 3. Other factual errors

- **The pilot ran for six months, not twelve.** It ran October 2025 to March 2026, but the conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot."
- **The membership rise is real but not attributable to the new hours.** 1,140 against 690 is +65%, so "about two-thirds" is right. But it covers all new members at the branch, with no comparison group. Did the other four branches see a rise over the same months? Was there a membership drive or a novelty effect? Without that comparison, the rise shows the branch did well during the pilot, not that the new hours caused it.

### 4. The visit estimate assumes every branch is Ashgrove

The 84,000 visits check out against Ashgrove's figures: (6 × 21 + 4 × 52) × 50 weeks × 5 branches ≈ 83,500. But Section 7 says Ashgrove is the busiest branch and demand elsewhere may be lower. The headline figure is therefore an upper bound.

| Scenario | Annual visits | Cost per visit (£164k) |
|---|---|---|
| All five at Ashgrove rates | 83,500 | £1.96 |
| Other four at 75% of Ashgrove | 66,800 | £2.46 |
| Other four at 50% of Ashgrove | 50,100 | £3.27 |

There are two further problems:
- **Displacement.** Some visits in the new hours are probably people who would otherwise have come during the day. The pilot data could test this: did Ashgrove's weekday or Saturday visits fall compared with the year before?
- **Unlike comparison.** The £3.40 borough average is an *average* cost, including buildings, stock and management. The ~£2 figure is a *marginal* cost. Comparing them makes the bid look better value than it is. A better comparison is marginal cost per visit against other ways of reaching working-age residents.

### 5. Costing points

- **Utilities are scaled from winter.** The pilot ran October to March, when heating and lighting peak. Scaling winter costs to a full year probably overstates the annual figure. That errs on the expensive side, but it is still a scaled estimate, not "actual pilot spend" as the author describes it.
- **The staffing rate needs a breakdown.** £24.80 includes "an enhancement for Sunday working." If the enhancement is applied to all ten hours, the evening hours are overcosted. If it is blended in proportion, say so and show the working.
- **The kiosk upgrades are unexplained.** Self-service kiosk maintenance appears in a bid for *staffed* hours, after self-service opening was rejected. What is it for?
- **Bank holiday weeks may be overstated.** The extra hours fall on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays, and most bank holidays are Mondays. If few of the extra hours are actually lost, 52 weeks may be more accurate, which would add about £5,000.

### 6. The self-service comparison is incomplete

The author's description says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The document doesn't show that:
- **Saving:** cutting staffing by about two-thirds saves roughly £83,000 a year.
- **Cost:** building works are £60,000 × 5 = £300,000, one-off and capital.
- **Payback:** about 3.6 years. After that, self-service is cheaper every year.

So self-service costs more in year one and less from about year four. The document's stronger argument is the second one: unstaffed hours can't host the job club or family activities. That argument should lead.

A hybrid deserves a line too. For example, staffed Sundays and job-club evenings, with self-service in the other evening hours or none.

### What holds up

- A real pilot of the exact opening pattern is better evidence than most growth bids have.
- Sunday demand is strong and well evidenced.
- The job club filling up from its third week is concrete evidence of evening value.
- The lone-working staffing requirement is properly costed.
- The risk about lower demand at other branches is acknowledged, though not carried through into the figures.

### Recommended changes

1. Correct the total to £164,000, or identify the missing line.
2. Replace "evening close to daytime" with the actual figures. Present Sunday as the strong result and evenings as moderate.
3. Correct "twelve-month" to six months.
4. Show visits and cost per visit under lower-demand scenarios for the other four branches, and test for displacement.
5. Compare marginal cost with marginal cost, not with the borough average.
6. Explain the kiosk line and break down the staffing rate.
7. Present self-service over several years, and consider phasing: Sundays at all five branches first, evenings where demand or the job club justifies them.

On the pilot evidence, Sunday opening at all five branches looks well justified. The full package may be too, but the bid needs to show it on corrected figures.
